reviews.body:
## Intent Publish the project's benchmark results: (1) a cross-engine 'Benchmarks' table in the main README showing, per query class, where MySQL 5.7 workloads regress or improve on each migration candidate (5.7→8.0 and 5.7→MariaDB 10.11, Δp95 plus Δmean where the source reports emphasize it), with regressions visually distinct via plain-text-friendly markers (bold + sign, not color-only); (2) the three executed benchmark writeups ported into docs/benchmarks/ (2026-07-16-mysql80-general.md, 2026-07-16-mysql80-hugetext.md, 2026-07-16-mariadb.md) and linked from the table and from docs/quickstart.md. The writeups are faithful ports of internal executed reports, scrubbed of internal references; every number was transcribed exactly from the source reports and verified — numeric values in the table and writeups are ground truth from real runs and must not be 'corrected'. Required footnotes kept deliberately: the 8.0 general run was stock-charset (charset confound deliberate — baselines labeled latin1-5.7 vs utf8mb4-5.7); blob MB/s absolutes are not comparable across tool versions (sql-replay 0.2.0 vs 0.4.0 memory model); all numbers are WSL2 ratios, not production absolutes; MariaDB sql_mode behavioral diffs called out as the real migration gotcha. The story the table tells: 8.0's group-by/temp-table cliff (up to ~5x, tunable) vs MariaDB's -15% on the same class; blob transfer at par on both; per-statement overhead on tiny queries as 8.0's other loss. A prior run raised the ask-user finding 'quickstart-charset-alone-overclaim' about docs/quickstart.md; the user decided: attribute the ~5x GROUP BY slowdown to stock 8.0 defaults (utf8mb4 default + TempTable on-disk spill), NOT 'charset alone' and NOT 'largely charset-driven' — that decided fix is already applied as the branch's pipeline fix commit 4e8e2c3 (no-mistakes(review): reword quickstart GROUP BY slowdown attribution to stock defaults); the finding is resolved and must not re-surface. The remaining 'charset alone costs 5.7 about +68% p95' statements in README/mariadb writeup are a different, accurate measured claim (5.7-latin1 vs 5.7-utf8mb4 baseline pair) and are intentional. Docs-only change; code, tests, and lint untouched. ## What Changed - Added a "Benchmarks" section to the README with a cross-engine table showing per-query-class Δp95 (plus Δmean where the source reports emphasize it) for MySQL 5.7→8.0 and 5.7→MariaDB 10.11 migrations, with regressions marked bold-with-sign so they read without color; load-bearing footnotes cover the 8.0 general run's stock-charset baseline labeling, the cross-tool-version blob MB/s caveat, and WSL2 ratios-not-absolutes. - Ported three executed benchmark writeups into `docs/benchmarks/` (`2026-07-16-mysql80-general.md`, `2026-07-16-mysql80-hugetext.md`, `2026-07-16-mariadb.md`), linked from the README table and `docs/quickstart.md`; every number is transcribed from real runs. Also reworded the quickstart's ~5x GROUP BY slowdown attribution to stock 8.0 defaults (utf8mb4 + TempTable on-disk spill) rather than charset alone, and per pipeline review corrected the checksum-match claim to 14 deterministic of 16 checked fingerprints in the README and MariaDB writeup. - Noted the `docs/benchmarks/` executed-writeup convention in `AGENTS.md` (numbers come from real runs, never hand-edited; new runs get new dated files). Docs-only change: the pipeline confirmed no code was touched, all 47 relative links and every table/prose number cross-check against the source writeups, and both new sections render correctly under GitHub's markdown renderer. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: Docs-only change; the single prior finding (checked-vs-deterministic checksum count) was fixed as instructed in both files, all table numbers match their source writeups, and all cross-file links and anchors resolve. ## Testing Exercised the docs the way a reader would: checked every relative link and anchor (47/47 resolve), cross-checked every README benchmark table cell and prose number against the executed writeups (all match, including bold regression markers and the corrected 14-of-16 checksum count), confirmed the decided quickstart wording and scrubbing constraints, and captured GitHub-rendered screenshots of the table and a writeup — everything passes; cargo tests skipped as the diff contains no code. - Evidence: README Benchmarks section rendered as GitHub-flavored markdown (table, bold regression markers, footnotes) (local file: /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/01KXNW5Z6V9GCMM5N2SYGYQD3Y/readme-benchmarks-render.png) - Evidence: MariaDB writeup rendered (header, verdict, general-workload results table) (local file: /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/01KXNW5Z6V9GCMM5N2SYGYQD3Y/mariadb-writeup-render.png)
Evidence: Number cross-check output: README table vs writeup ground truth `All 12 table rows OK (Δp95 + bold flags, both columns) + 9 prose checks OK (gb 202→1145 / 340→289, +68% charset delta, checksum 14-of-16, Δmean parentheticals, MB/s footnote) → ALL CONSISTENT` ```text OK join + GROUP BY over VARCHAR keys 8.0 +465% bold=True (want +465%,True) | maria -15% bold=False (want -15%,False) OK pk point lookup 8.0 +8% bold=False (want +8%,False) | maria -3% bold=False (want -3%,False) OK hire-date secondary-index lookup 8.0 -6% bold=False (want -6%,False) | maria -4% bold=False (want -4%,False) OK short INSERT (audit row) 8.0 +25% bold=True (want +25%,True) | maria +5% bold=False (want +5%,False) OK full fetch 100KB 8.0 -16% bold=False (want -16%,False) | maria -4% bold=False (want -4%,False) OK full fetch 1MB 8.0 +5% bold=False (want +5%,False) | maria -7% bold=False (want -7%,False) OK full fetch 5MB 8.0 -18% bold=False (want -18%,False) | maria +5% bold=False (want +5%,False) OK full fetch 15MB 8.0 +4% bold=False (want +4%,False) | maria +10% bold=False (want +10%,False) OK full fetch 100KB 8.0 +34% bold=True (want +34%,True) | maria +16% bold=False (want +16%,False) OK full fetch 1MB 8.0 -5% bold=False (want -5%,False) | maria +23% bold=True (want +23%,True) OK full fetch 5MB 8.0 -9% bold=False (want -9%,False) | maria +8% bold=False (want +8%,False) OK full fetch 15MB 8.0 -9% bold=False (want -9%,False) | maria +6% bold=False (want +6%,False) OK README gb 8.0 abs OK README gb maria abs OK README +68% charset delta OK README checksum 14 of 16 OK insert mean +7% OK gb maria mean -15% OK 15MB C1 maria mean +10% OK 1MB C12 maria mean +18% OK MB/s cross-version footnote ALL CONSISTENT ```

reviews.body:
## Summary

- Rewrites the README from 557 to 215 lines around a problem-first hook, demo, install, token economics, and three differentiated capabilities.
- Updates all launch copy to the verified current surfaces: 38/55/159 MCP tools, ~3.8k/~5.0k/~18k schema tokens, and 135 CLI commands.
- Adds a tracked launch pack for Show HN, Reddit, objection handling, and awesome-list submissions.
- Changes documentation only; no source, test, script, or hook files are modified.

## Content migration map

Nothing removed from the old README was left without a reference destination:

- Offline/network policy → `PRIVACY.md` (corrected to document the default-on throttled update tag check and its opt-out).
- Token-saving techniques and ROI semantics → `docs/reference.md#configuration` / Token economy.
- Use cases → new `docs/reference.md#use-cases`.
- Ambient recall, auto-capture, session briefing, visible context → `docs/reference.md#ambient-memory` and `#surfaces`.
- Cross-agent resume + screenshot → `docs/reference.md#surfaces`.
- Dream phases, receipts, synthesis, and optional self-improvement flags → `docs/reference.md#surfaces`.
- Cross-Mac git sync and Obsidian-as-source-of-truth → `docs/reference.md#surfaces`.
- Knowledge graph commands, codegraph traceability, and feature flags → existing expanded sections under `#ambient-memory` and `#cli-reference`.
- Temporal facts, health/eval gates, multimodal ingestion, and secret storage → `docs/reference.md#surfaces`.
- Daemon table and complete 135-command inventory → `docs/reference.md#cli-reference`.
- MCP profile table and authenticated localhost HTTP API → `docs/reference.md#mcp-tools`.
- Embedding model matrix → existing, more complete `docs/reference.md#configuration`.
- Full 14-row comparison, architecture, Memo 4 independence, license, and provenance → `docs/reference.md#design-and-comparison`.
- Requirements and measured benchmark table → `docs/reference.md#install-detail`.

The required anchors already existed and were preserved: `install-detail`, `mcp-setup`, `mcp-tools`, `ambient-memory`, `surfaces`, `cli-reference`, `configuration`, and `design-and-comparison`.

## Verification findings

- README relative links/anchors: 15 checked, all resolve.
- README external URLs: 18 checked with redirect following, all returned HTTP 200.
- Assets:
  - `docs/banner.jpg`: 372,301 bytes — exceeds the requested 200 KB launch budget and should be optimized.
  - `docs/demo.gif`: 152,101 bytes.
  - `docs/diagram-recall.svg`: 3,893 bytes.
- Demo GIF: 673 frames, 26.92 seconds — below the 30-second launch blocker.
- MCP surfaces: verified from real server registration as agent 38, core/slim 55, full/default 159; token labels ~3.8k/~5.0k/~18k.
- ROI copy: removed the unsupported “~80k per session” corpus-size extrapolation. `memo roi` actually reads grounding/re-ask ledgers and defaults to 350 tokens per grounded recall plus 900 per avoided re-ask.
- CLI surface: 135 top-level commands; README and reference inventories exactly match the Click registry.
- `shellcheck`: unavailable on this machine. `bash -n install.sh` passes; `install.sh` was not modified.
- Focused verification: 12 tests passed for MCP counts, schema labels, CLI inventory, hook budget, and ROI formula.
- Push gate: `memo eval recall --gate --profile pre-push` passed (`prec@k 0.714`, `noise@k 0.000`).

## Commits

1. `docs(reference): migrate detailed sections from README`
2. `docs(readme): rewrite for conversion — problem-first hook, demo above the fold`
3. `docs(launch): add launch pack — Show HN, reddit angles, objection handling`
4. `docs(readme): restore versioned installer examples for release check`

Not merging; awaiting review.

reviews.body: See [Commits](/coleleavitt/codegraph/pull/19/commits) and [Changes](/coleleavitt/codegraph/pull/19/files) for more details. ----- Created by [ **pull[bot]**](https://github.com/wei/pull) (v2.0.0-alpha.4) _Can you help keep this open source service alive? **[💖 Please sponsor : )](https://prod.download/pull-pr-sponsor)**_ --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes token accounting in the eval harness and refreshes benchmark results using a CLI-blocked methodology, removing undercounting and updating the README numbers. Across seven repos with CodeGraph: 88% fewer tool calls, 53% faster, 62% fewer tokens, 44% cheaper, and zero file reads. - **Bug Fixes** - Sum “tokens processed” per assistant turn and dedupe by `message.id` in `parse-run.mjs` (no longer read the last-turn-only `result.usage`). - Block the `codegraph` CLI in both arms (sanitized `PATH` + PreToolUse) to prevent control-arm contamination; contamination is tracked and reported. - **Docs** - README benchmark table re-measured on `claude-opus-4-8` with the corrected harness; per-repo medians and methodology updated. - `docs/benchmarks/residual-context-occupancy.md`: token column corrected (average tokens saved now 56%); cost, time, and tool-call figures unchanged; occupancy findings stand. - `docs/benchmarks/call-sequence-analysis.md`: notes the prior undercount issue and how it affected results; guidance on summing per-turn usage. - `docs/benchmarks/answer-directly-vs-explore-agent.md`: flags earlier token figures as indicative due to missing raw logs. Written for commit d6d17288beedc1076b1cc1825db307f6455c9f98. Summary will update on new commits.

added_numeric_lines: +> **A note on cost:** CodeGraph's win on *every* codebase is precision — the agent stops crawling files and answers from the graph. On current models that precision is also a large direct saving: the 2026-08 re-measurement, on a harness that blocks the CLI in both arms, put it at **44% lower cost and 62% fewer tokens on average** across the seven benchmark repos, because a strong model *without* the graph burns its budget re-deriving structure. Cost tracks how much *discovery* a question demands more than raw repo size: 57–78% on questions the file-reading agent needed 28–43 tool calls to answer, near-even where it got there in 7.

+Tested across **7 real-world open-source codebases** spanning 7 languages, comparing an agent (Claude Code, headless) answering one architecture question **with** and **without** CodeGraph, at the **median of 4 runs per arm**. _Re-measured 2026-08-05 on **Claude Opus 4.8** against the current build, on a harness that blocks the `codegraph` CLI in **both** arms — contamination row: 0 of 28 without-arm runs._
+> **The universal win — every repo, every size: 88% fewer tool calls · 53% faster · 62% fewer tokens · 44% cheaper · file reads cut to zero on all seven repos.**

+With the index available, the agent answers from one to four `codegraph_explore` calls and stops. Without it, the agent burns its budget on discovery — up to **43 tool calls and 19 file reads** re-deriving what the graph already knew. Every repo was faster with CodeGraph in this measurement — by 35% on the narrowest question, by 3.6× on the widest.
+| **VS Code** | TypeScript · ~11k files | **2 vs 28** | **2.2× faster** (58s vs 2m 10s) | **0** vs 12 | 77% fewer | 71% cheaper |
+| **Excalidraw** | TypeScript · ~640 | **2 vs 43** | **3.6× faster** (45s vs 2m 42s) | **0** vs 18 | 84% fewer | 78% cheaper |
+| **Django** | Python · ~3k | 3 vs 14 | 35% faster (54s vs 1m 23s) | **0** vs 8.5 | 41% fewer | 13% cheaper¹ |
+| **Tokio** | Rust · ~790 | 3 vs 29 | **2.6× faster** (1m 3s vs 2m 43s) | **0** vs 19 | 65% fewer | 64% cheaper |
+| **OkHttp** | Java · ~645 | 1 vs 6 | 43% faster (33s vs 58s) | **0** vs 2 | 54% fewer | 21% cheaper |
+| **Gin** | Go · ~110 | 1 vs 7 | 39% faster (28s vs 46s) | **0** vs 4 | 52% fewer | ~even¹ |
+| **Alamofire** | Swift · ~110 | 4 vs 33 | **2.6× faster** (54s vs 2m 22s) | **0** vs 16.5 | 59% fewer | 57% cheaper |

+<sub>¹ Cost tracks how much *discovery* the question demanded, which is why it varies far more than the other columns: 57–78% on repos where the file-reading arm needed 28–43 tool calls, but only 13% on Django and even on Gin, where it got there in 14 and 7. The with-arm still answered in 3 and 1 calls with zero file reads. **File reads** = median files opened — the surgical-context win in one column: the agent never reads a file on any of the seven repos when CodeGraph is present.</sub>

+**Methodology.** Each arm is `claude -p` (Claude Opus 4.8, `claude-opus-4-8`) run headlessly against the repo with `--strict-mcp-config`: **WITH** = CodeGraph's MCP server enabled, **WITHOUT** = an empty MCP config. Built-in Read/Grep/Bash stay available to both. Same question per repo, **4 runs per arm, median reported**. Cost = the run's `total_cost_usd`; Tokens = total tokens processed, summed per assistant turn (input incl. cache reads + cache creation + output); Time = wall-clock; Tool calls = every tool invocation, including those inside any sub-agents the model spawns. Repos cloned at `--depth 1` and indexed by the same CodeGraph build that served them. Re-measured 2026-08-05 on the current build.

+**The `codegraph` CLI is blocked in both arms.** A sanitized `PATH` plus a `PreToolUse` hook denies any Bash invocation of the CLI, in the WITHOUT arm as well as the WITH arm. This matters: without that block the control arm is not a control. On an unblocked harness we measured the WITHOUT agent finding the CLI on `PATH` and reaching CodeGraph through Bash in **26 of 28 runs** — which distorts the comparison in both directions, since a CLI call is not counted as a tool call and its output still enters the window. Earlier published figures were produced without this block. In the run reported above, all 28 WITHOUT runs attempted the CLI and **all 28 were blocked — 0 contaminated**.
removed_numeric_lines: -> **A note on cost:** CodeGraph's win on *every* codebase is precision — the agent stops crawling files and answers from the graph. On current models that precision is also a large direct saving: the 2026-07 re-validation measured **60% lower cost and 69% fewer tokens on average** across the seven benchmark repos, because a strong model *without* the graph burns millions of tokens re-deriving structure. The savings scale with repo size and tangle — dramatic on VS-Code-class trees, modest on a 100-file project — and compound across a team's daily agent usage.

-Tested across **7 real-world open-source codebases** spanning 7 languages, comparing an agent (Claude Code, headless) answering one architecture question **with** and **without** CodeGraph, at the **median of 4 runs per arm**. _Re-validated 2026-07-21 on **Claude Opus 4.8** against the current build — the Rust kernel plus this cycle's resolution overhaul._
-> **The universal win — every repo, every size: 89% fewer tool calls · 60% cheaper · 69% fewer tokens · file reads cut to zero on all seven repos.**

-With the index available, the agent answers from a couple of `codegraph_explore` calls and stops. Without it, the agent burns its budget on discovery — up to **57 tool calls and 4.3M tokens** re-deriving what the graph already knew. The **Time** column averages 20% faster but is the noisiest metric: on two small repos a strong model's raw grep loop finishes the wall-clock race sooner while still spending 5–10× the tokens and money — noted per-row below.

-| **Alamofire** | Swift · ~110 | 3 vs 53 | 49s vs 31s¹ | **0** vs 18 | 90% fewer | 86% cheaper |

-<sub>¹ The small-repo floor effect: Opus 4.8 greps small trees fast enough to win wall-clock while spending ~5–10× the tokens and ~4–7× the cost — the with-arm still answers from zero file reads. ² OkHttp's without-arm got lucky in 5 calls; the with-arm answered in 1 call for ~$0.03 more. **File reads** = median files opened — the surgical-context win in one column: the agent never reads a file on any of the seven repos when CodeGraph is present.</sub>

Built-in Read/Grep/Bash stay available to both. Same question per repo, **4 runs per arm, median reported**. Cost = the run's `total_cost_usd`; Tokens = total tokens processed (input incl. cached + output); Time = wall-clock; Tool calls = every tool invocation, including those inside any sub-agents the model spawns. reviews.body:
## 📊 Phase 2: Real Baseline Harness

**Follows**: PR #114 (Phase 1 - Unicode Correctness, merged)  
**Type**: Infrastructure / Baseline  
**Status**: Phase 2 Implementation Complete - Ready for merge

---

## 🎯 What This PR Does

Implements Phase 2 of the Performance Optimization RFC: a reproducible baseline harness that generates statistical performance data with complete environment information.

**This PR does NOT include optimizations** - it establishes the measurement foundation required before any optimization work.

---

## 📦 Implementation

### Baseline Harness Features

```bash
pnpm run bench:perf-baseline        # Display results to console
pnpm run bench:perf-baseline:json   # Save to .tmp/perf-baseline.json
pnpm run bench:perf-baseline:smoke  # Quick validation (~2-3s)
```

**Key Features**:
- ✅ Statistical analysis: p50/p95/p99, mean, stdev, CV, stability classification
- ✅ **Schema version**: v1 with benchmarkSuite identifier
- ✅ Environment capture: commit, EAW Unicode + runtime Unicode/ICU, V8, OS, CPU
- ✅ Reproducible clock: `process.hrtime.bigint`
- ✅ **Blackhole sink**: Prevents V8 optimization elimination
- ✅ **Dynamic unique corpus**: True cache-miss path (not cycling)
- ✅ Structured JSON output with `ns/op` (nanoseconds per operation)
- ✅ Sanity checks before benchmarking
- ✅ CLI/env parameter validation
- ✅ Smoke mode integrated in `release:bench`

### 18 Benchmark Scenarios

**Character width calculations** (5):
1. `charCellWidth_ascii` - ASCII (a, Z, 0)
2. `charCellWidth_bmp_cjk` - BMP CJK (中, 文, 字)
3. `charCellWidth_supplementary_cjk` - Supplementary CJK (𠮷, Ext E/G)
4. `charCellWidth_non_cjk_supplementary` - Musical/math symbols
5. `charCellWidth_emoji_sequence` - Emoji with ZWJ

**Text width operations** (7):
6. `textCellWidth_ascii_long_fast_path` - ASCII 100 chars (fast path bypass)
7. `textCellWidth_ascii_unique` - Unique ASCII (still fast path, not cache)
8. `textCellWidth_cjk_long_hot` - BMP CJK 100 chars (hot cache)
9. `textCellWidth_cjk_unique` - Unique CJK (cache-miss path)
10. `textCellWidth_supplementary_cjk_long_hot` - Supplementary CJK 50 chars
11. **`textCellWidth_complex_grapheme_hot`** - ZWJ emoji, combining marks (hot cache)
12. **`textCellWidth_complex_grapheme_unique`** - Complex grapheme (tests segmentedGraphemes)

**Text operations** (4):
13. **`harness_blackhole_overhead`** - Blackhole overhead baseline (informational)
14. `sliceByCells_supplementary_cjk` - Slicing operations
15. `wrapByCells_cjk_long_hot` - Text wrapping (hot cache)
16. `wrapByCells_cjk_unique` - Text wrapping (cache-miss path)

**Terminal integration** (2):
17. `terminal_write_supplementary_cjk_hot` - Same position (hot Cell cache)
18. `terminal_write_supplementary_cjk_cycling_rows` - Cycling rows

---

## 🔧 Key Improvements from Reviews

### Complex Grapheme Coverage ✅
Added 2 scenarios testing `segmentedGraphemes` path:
- ZWJ emoji (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦, 👩‍💻)
- Regional indicators (🇺🇸)
- Combining marks (é = e + U+0301)
- Tests Intl.Segmenter fallback

Essential for Phase 3 if grapheme optimization considered.

### True Cache-Miss Path ✅
**Not** "no-cache" (misleading). Scenarios:
- ✅ Execute cache lookup (miss)
- ✅ Execute cache insertion
- ✅ Execute LRU eviction
- ✅ Model unique log lines accurately

Dynamic corpus: `(warmup + samples) * iterations + 100`
- Smoke: ~104 entries
- Full: ~11,100 entries
- No cycling/wrapping

### ASCII Fast Path Clarification ✅
`textCellWidth` bypasses cache for ASCII:
```typescript
if (hasAsciiFastPath(provider) && isAscii(text)) return text.length;
```

- `textCellWidth_ascii_long_fast_path`: Fast path (no cache)
- `textCellWidth_ascii_unique`: Still fast path (no cache), just unique input

Neither tests text cache. For cache-miss testing, see CJK unique scenarios.

### Blackhole Overhead ✅
`harness_blackhole_overhead` measures pure harness cost.
- **Informational only**
- **Not subtracted** from results
- Helps interpret ultra-small ns/op

### Schema Version ✅
```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "benchmarkSuite": "unicode-width-text-v1"
}
```
Future-proof for Phase 3+ metrics additions.

---

## 📋 Output Format

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "benchmarkSuite": "unicode-width-text-v1",
  "commit": "...",
  "eawUnicodeVersion": "17.0.0",
  "runtimeUnicodeVersion": "15.1.0",
  "icu": "75.1",
  "node": "v24.16.0",
  "v8": "13.6.233.17",
  "os": "darwin-arm64",
  "cpu": "Apple M1 Pro",
  "warmup": 100,
  "samples": 1000,
  "clock": "process.hrtime.bigint",
  "timestamp": "2026-07-09T...",
  "blackhole": 12345,
  "results": {
    "charCellWidth_ascii": {
      "p50": 3.90,
      "p95": 8.13,
      "p99": 8.21,
      "mean": 4.28,
      "stdev": 1.20,
      "cv": 0.2793,
      "stability": "noisy",
      "samples": 1000,
      "unit": "ns/op",
      "iterationsPerSample": 1000,
      "operationsPerIteration": 3
    }
  }
}
```

---

## ⚠️ Important Limitations

This harness covers **Unicode width/text operation micro-benchmarks**. It does NOT fully cover:
- **Cache tuning workloads** (need Cell allocation/GC instrumentation)
- **Virtual scroll scenarios** (need rendering workloads)
- **Real application workloads** (need integration benchmarks)

**Per RFC**: Phase 3 optimization PRs must provide **targeted baseline + profiler evidence** for their specific optimization area.

Current terminal scenarios only test buffer write (no commit/render). They cannot prove Cell cache tuning is beneficial without instrumentation showing:
- createCell call count
- new Cell allocation count
- Cache hit/miss rates
- map.clear() frequency
- Live Style distribution
- Heap delta / GC pressure

---

## 📝 Next Steps (Phase 3)

**Profiler/Instrumentation PR** (NOT optimization yet):
- Add debug-only metrics
- Measure Cell cache behavior
- Measure text cache behavior  
- Identify proven bottlenecks
- **Observation only, no behavior changes**

**Only after profiler evidence**:
- Cache tuning (if proven bottleneck)
- Long text strategy (if proven bottleneck)
- Virtual scroll (if proven bottleneck)

---

## ✅ Phase 2 Completion Criteria

Per RFC requirements:

- ✅ Unified harness (single script, consistent methodology)
- ✅ Statistical metrics (p50/p95/p99/mean/stdev/CV + stability)
- ✅ Environment info (commit, EAW + runtime Unicode, V8, OS, CPU, ICU)
- ✅ JSON output (structured, versioned format)
- ✅ Reproducible (deterministic clock, fixed warmup/samples, blackhole sink)
- ✅ Key scenarios (character width, text ops hot/cache-miss, complex grapheme, terminal)
- ✅ Documentation (usage, metrics, interpretation, limitations)
- ✅ Sanity checks (prevent wrong-behavior benchmarks)
- ✅ Smoke mode (CI validation)
- ✅ Parameter validation (fail-fast on invalid input)

---

**Type**: Infrastructure  
**Breaking Changes**: None  
**Status**: Ready for merge  
**Next**: Phase 3 profiler/instrumentation (separate PR, no optimization yet)

reviews.body:
The published benchmark answers "is culprit accurate". That is the wrong question now that any coding agent can run `git blame` itself. This runs the honest one.

Three arms, same 10 regressions (5 git, 5 systemd), same scoring:

| | culprit alone | agent alone | agent + culprit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Introducing commit ranked #1 | 80% | **90%** | **90%** |
| Introducing commit in top 5 | 90% | **100%** | **100%** |
| Mean tool calls | n/a | 15.0 | **8.9** |

## What it found, including the part that is not flattering

**The agent beats culprit, and culprit does not make the agent more accurate.** 90% vs 80% top-1, and adding culprit leaves accuracy at 90%. Any claim that culprit finds root causes better than a capable agent is not supported.

**What culprit does is cut the work.** 41% fewer tool calls and 14% fewer tokens, lower in 9 of 9 matched cases with no reversals, and 42 calls down to 16 on the hardest case. culprit itself costs no tokens and runs in under a second. So it is an accelerator for an agent, not a replacement for one, and the README now says exactly that.

**It is not just anchoring the agent.** Arm C reordered culprit's ranking in 7 of 10 cases. On case 04, where culprit's top suspect was wrong, the agent rejected it and found the right commit by running `make -qp` to compare the default goal at HEAD and at its parent, which is evidence a history-only engine cannot produce.

## Fairness

Ground truth is each fix's `Fixes:` trailer, so an agent that can reach the fix commit just reads the answer. Every case runs in a `--shared` clone rewound to the fix's parent with all other refs, the remote and the reflog stripped. Verified per sandbox: fix not an ancestor of HEAD, one ref only, no history search surfaces the expected SHA, and the introducing commit is still reachable so the case stays solvable. Both arms get the diff and nothing else, matching what `pr_context.from_local` hands culprit (`title=None, body=None`), and both are scored by `run.py`'s own `score_case`.

## Also in here

- Drops a README line claiming an agent "cannot see" that a bug came from an old refactor. This benchmark disproves it.
- Fixes a `.gitignore` bug: a bare `benchmarks` line ignored the whole directory. Tracked files survived only because gitignore does not apply to the index, so it was invisible until adding a new file. The specific cache and results rules are kept and verified.

## Limits, stated in the harness README too

n=10; this slice is easier than the full 50 (culprit scores 80% here vs 50% there), so only the between-arm comparison is meaningful; cases 26 and 27 share an introducing commit; arm B never fell below top 5, so there is no evidence culprit rescues a failing agent; and `verify_fix` is untested by this benchmark.

  - Added benchmark documentation covering methodology, fairness rules, limitations, reproduction steps, and expected outputs.

- **Benchmarks**
  - Added evaluation results comparing culprit-only, agent-only, and combined workflows across regression cases.
  - Added isolated benchmark setup and scoring utilities for reproducible analysis.

## What

Combines the two JavaScript-performance roadmaps into a single [`docs/performance-roadmap.md`](docs/performance-roadmap.md), then works through phase 0 against the tree.

| Merged from | Contributed |
|---|---|
| `Broiler.JS/docs/performance-roadmap.md` | The engine-internal P0–P3 campaign, its measurements, and the open items each phase left behind |
| `tests/octane/roadmap.md` | The forward plan Octane 2.0 argues for — phases 0–5, ordered by where the suite says the losses are |
| `tests/octane/benchmarks.md` | The ranked blockers B1–B8 that connect the two |

## Why here, and why one document

The two overlap heavily — Octane's phase 2 items *are* the engine roadmap's open items — and they **disagree in one place**, which nobody could see while they sat apart.

It lives in the parent because the plan spans both trees: the harness is main-repo (`tests/octane`, `scripts`, the workflow) and the engine is a submodule. A document inside the submodule cannot link out to the harness, so only the parent can hold the combined view.

Both sources are left in place. The engine one remains the archive of record for the detailed defect narratives this drops as history rather than plan.

## The two findings the merge produces

**1. The engine roadmap's scope statement is wrong, and Octane is why.** Its §9 excludes *parsing and compilation* and *a real JIT* as out of scope, reasoning from probes that showed fresh-context startup at 1.20 ms. But Octane's two worst scores measure nothing but the front end — **MandreelLatency at 4646×** and **CodeLoad at 371×**. Eager compilation is free on a one-line probe and is not free on jQuery or a 152,948-line generated function. The probe corpus was too small to see it. Both exclusions are superseded and become phases 1 and 4.

**2. Both roadmaps are blocked on the same gate**, described two ways: one owes a workflow run, the other acceptance evidence. Merged into a single phase 0.

## Phase 0

Items were **checked against the tree rather than inherited**, which caught two wrong claims:

- **0-9 was recorded as "not created."** The benchmark project already existed and was already the configured `benchmark.project`; the missing part was the corpus inside it. Added in Broiler-Platform/Broiler.JS#938, which this bumps the pointer to.
- **The pinned pointer both documents name (`cdb2fd41`) is stale by 7 commits.** All three patch commits remain ancestors, so the item's substance holds — but every measurement the documents report was taken there and has not been repeated at `b3f53dcc`.

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| 0-1 … 0-5 | **Done**, verified in the tree |
| 0-6 (Octane workflow run) | **Needs CI** — cannot be dispatched from a checkout |
| 0-7 (benchmark comparison) | **Done** — both named classes plus the new probes, 2 repetitions, win-x64 |
| 0-8 (RID matrix inside the band) | **Not satisfiable here** — see below |
| 0-9 (probe corpus) | **Done** |
| 0-10, 0-11 | Already done |

## Reviewer notes

**0-8 failed the band, and that is the protocol working.** The win-x64 leg ran and reported `withinNoiseBand: False` — **25 of 62 metrics outside 7.5%**, worst 56%. It was run on a 16-core developer workstation; `performance.md` requires an *idle physical machine*. Recorded as unsatisfiable locally rather than quietly reported as a pass.

**A local Broiler-only Octane pass answers most of 0-6.** All five previously-failing suites now score — Crypto, PdfJS, CodeLoad, zlib and Typescript — confirming those fixes in the engine rather than by inspection.

**It also found one new failure.** Mandreel dies in `Setup` with the engine's own stack guard and a **six-frame JavaScript stack**, which is item 1-2's exact signature: the engine recursing over `global_init`, not the program recursing. That item had no live repro; it has one now, and it is the only thing between the suite and 17 of 17 scores. Whether it is a regression in the last 7 commits or a Linux-vs-Windows difference needs the CI run to separate. Notably it is *contained* — exit code 0, other 14 suites unaffected — where the same overflow used to take a whole suite down.

Those scores are **not** comparable to the committed Chromium column (different hardware, 7 commits ahead) and are not presented as a geomean or spread. Only the pass/fail column is read, which is hardware-independent.

**The new corpus caught documentation drift on its first run.** §4.1's table shows the empty loop at 96 B/iter and integer arithmetic at 128 B/iter, before *and* after P0. Both now allocate **zero** — P2-2 item 3 landed afterward. The prose says so; the headline table never got updated.

## Risk

Documentation plus a benchmark-only submodule bump. No engine or product code is touched.

Corrects `docs/decisions/verification-moves-from-open-to-touch.md`, merged an
hour ago in PR #763. Raised by the owner reading the summary and stopping on one
phrase.

## The error

The record said the eager verification is **"one call in one function"** and
named `dashbuf::open`. There are two, in two functions, on two paths — and it
named the wrong one for the case the slice is about.

`prefix::Plan::bind` hashes every fetched payload against the section table
([`crates/dashbuf/src/prefix.rs:356`](https://github.com/driftsys/dashscene-staging/blob/eb0c095926a26f73a931a91931994bfed8651f23/crates/dashbuf/src/prefix.rs#L354-L358)).
**Since story #596 that is the one that runs over a mapping.** The native mapped
host reads its envelope with `prefix`, plans, and calls `bind` for its check;
`dashbuf::open` is left holding the embedded golden, which is a `&'static [u8]`
with no pages to fault.

So the function the record was written about is, on the only path where a
mapping exists, no longer the function doing the damage. **Moving only `open`
would have left the criterion at 9.81x** and made story #597 look like it had
failed.

## What changed

- **D7 is now `Plan::bind`'s half.** Both readers give up their hashing to the
  same `Residency`, so a payload is proven in one place rather than two that
  could disagree. `bind` becomes the binding its name claims.
- **D8 is the counter** (was D7): `record_hashed` moves out of both readers.
- **D9 is new, and it is the other thing that would have gone wrong.** Story
  #598's benchmark measures `open_with_cost` plus
  `load_document_bound_with_cost` — the **owned** path. It writes its two
  documents to memory and maps nothing, so left alone it could not have seen any
  of this work. The re-run writes each generated document to a temporary file
  and maps it, which also makes the criterion a measurement of what a host does
  rather than of a path only the benchmark takes.
- **The title and scope** name both readers.
- **"faults every page of the file in" is corrected.** `open` reads the hot
  sections and every payload an entry names; a blob no entry names is never
  resolved, and the alignment padding between sections is never read. In this
  repository's documents that changes the wording rather than the conclusion,
  because blobs are nearly all of the bytes — but "the whole file" is a claim
  the code does not make.

**D1–D6 are unchanged.** The shape they chose was right; this is what it has to
be applied to.

## Why this got through

The record was checked by an agent told to verify every factual claim against
the code, and it verified the claims that were *made* — `open` does hash every
payload, `verify_hot` does exist and is not called, the quotations, the counts.
It did not ask the question nobody had written down: *is `open` still on the
path this slice cares about?* Story #596 had moved that path four hours earlier,
in a PR whose own description says so.

A claim can be true of the function it names and still be the wrong function.
Worth carrying into #599's records.

## Verification

Documentation only, two Markdown files. `just lint` green — `cargo fmt --check`,
`dprint check`, `markdownlint`, clippy.

## CI exception

**GitHub Actions cannot schedule a job on this account.** The owner authorised
merging on local evidence while this lasts, recorded per PR.

Refs #597. Refs #594.

reviews.body:
## Why

These files are not documentation. `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/pr-review/*` and
`.claude/skills/second-opinion/SKILL.md` are read by every `repo:api` worker and by every
`/pr-review` session, so a stale line here is an actively wrong order, not a docs nit.

They described machinery the harness rebuild retires: an unattended `--sleep` mode, a merge
sweep whose commit-anchored approval check was the blocking path, and a `check-lockstep.mjs`
that machine-compared the pr-review twins. A worker reading these looks for an approval gate
that will not run and assumes the twins are kept honest by a tool that is being deleted.

Companion to the orbit-ui-mobile branch `chore/harness-rebuild`. **Merge that one first.**

## Read this before merging: the rebuild has NOT landed

I verified this against live GitHub rather than trusting the plan, and two of the premises I
was handed were false. On orbit-ui-mobile `main` today, **all of these still exist**:

`tools/merge-sweep.sh` · `tools/merge-sweep-cov.sh` · `tools/check-lockstep.mjs` ·
`tools/lockstep-declarations.json` · `.claude/skills/llm-council/SKILL.md` · `tools/test-tools.mjs`

The rebuild that deletes them is committed only on a **local, unpushed** `chore/harness-rebuild`
branch. There is no orbit-ui-mobile PR. What *has* landed is the branch-protection change:
`Harness Lockstep` and `Skill and Agent Frontmatter` came off this repo's required contexts on
2026-08-04, leaving **13**.

So the prose here is written to be true in both states: the lockstep check is *being retired* and
already blocks nothing, rather than *already gone*.

## What changed

| file | was | now |

reviews.body:
## Description

**Summary:**
Correct the erroneous VAD benchmark row for Hood River segment `c1416cf1`, keep the
15s stream chunk as the sensitivity fixture while adding the 4.68s stitched payload
alongside it, and gate the suite on recall rather than F1 alone.

**Context & Motivation:**
The benchmark row for this file was wrong, and that is what made the fixture look
like it was missing speech. `VAD_BENCHMARKS.md` recorded Recall `1.000` under a
heading stating `pad_sec = 0.0`, but that `1.000` was measured at `pad_sec = 0.3`.
Holding everything but `pad_sec` constant:

| config | F1 | Precision | Recall |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| `pad_sec = 0.0` (benchmark table) | 0.791 | 0.687 | 0.932 |
| `pad_sec = 0.3` (production) | 0.794 | 0.659 | 1.000 |

The 0.068 gap at `0.0` is speech-edge clipping at `0.532s`, `5.696s`, and `6.672s`.
Production padding absorbs it entirely, so against the current annotation nothing is
clipped in shipped output.

The 15s chunk is retained as the sensitivity guard: Hood River is a `bcfy_feeds`
source, which the icecast collector cuts into `CHUNK_DURATION_SECONDS` windows, so
that is the audio shape the VAD receives in production. The 4.68s payload is a
downstream artifact whose boundaries come from a prior run of the detector under
test, so it is added as a second fixture rather than a replacement. Each fixture keeps its own hand-supplied annotation. They disagree on where the second burst starts — 11.268 in chunk coordinates versus 11.516 from the payload — and that 248ms is recorded in VAD_BENCHMARKS.md rather than resolved, since both are hand-supplied.

`_run_integration_test` gains an optional `min_recall` floor and now emits Precision
and Recall alongside F1, making CI output the source of truth for the table — F1
alone lets a recall drop hide behind the precision gain that clipping produces. A
production-padding test asserts Recall `1.000` on the chunk, since the high-recall
quality philosophy is about shipped output and a `pad_sec = 0.0` table cannot answer
that question.

**Future Work / Out of Scope:**
- The other twelve benchmark rows are unverified. One was demonstrably wrong, so they
  should be re-measured from CI output before being relied on.
- If the originally reported missed speech is real, it is speech absent from the
  current ground truth — Recall `1.000` at production padding only proves nothing
  *annotated* is clipped. Extending the annotation is the next step, ahead of any
  VAD threshold tuning for quiet vocal onsets.

---

## How Has This Been Tested?
- [x] Unit Tests (`uv run python -m pytest backend/pipeline/segmentation/tests/test_vad.py -n 0` — 35 passed)
- [x] Local manual testing (per-config metrics measured directly to confirm the
      `pad_sec` 0.0 vs 0.3 discrepancy and locate the clipped intervals)
- [ ] Data validation / Execution verified in staging

## Checklist
- [x] Self-review of my own code.
- [x] Commented code in hard-to-understand areas or complex logic.
- [x] Updated documentation.
- [x] Included any dependent changes that this PR is relying on in the description

reviews.body:
Round 1 of the review on [#260](https://github.com/pedrobzz/AckerDB/pull/260) (the 0.17.0 promotion). Two findings, both applied here so the release PR picks them up.

## System issuance could store a grant that widens later

The child invariant is enforced at both ends — subset at issuance, intersection at use — and `systemCredentials` honored only the second. `create` under a parent accepted any pattern, so `orders.*` stored against an identity holding `orders.read` looked correctly narrow and would begin authorizing `orders.write` the day that identity gained it, with nobody having granted the difference. Use-time intersection hides this precisely until it stops being true.

No escalation was ever possible — the intersection holds at every moment — so this is dormancy, not a bypass. But `child-credentials.ts` states the invariant holds at *both* ends, and one door did not.

System authority has no grant of its own to be bounded against, so issuance cannot be checked there the way `credentials.*` checks it. What can be held is the property the invariant exists for: **a concrete grant's expansion is fixed the moment it is stored**, so the scopes an operator names are the most that child can ever reach. Open-ended patterns under a parent now belong to the bounded door. A root credential has no parent to outgrow and keeps its patterns — tested both ways.

## The benchmark was documented in the wrong place

`docs/releases.md` is the authoritative procedure and still said `Fast CI` runs the benchmark and that a promotion is a no-op. That stopped being true when the promotion gate landed. Left alone, an agent reading it would restore the old shape believing the new one was the mistake — the same staleness trap this repo has been deliberate about avoiding. Both it and AGENTS.md now record where the check runs, why the promotion is the right place to measure (the comparison is the whole release delta, not one pull request's slice), and that it is required on `main`.

## Reviewed and left alone

**MCP tool-entry access is not a second authorization model.** `mcp/tool-access.ts` reuses `normalizeScopeRequirement` and `isScopeAuthorized` — the same primitives the function funnel uses — and adds `public`/`authenticated` handling for tool *entries*, which is a curation filter layered on top of the function's own `compileAccess`, not a replacement for it. Its one divergence, that system does not bypass a scoped tool entry, is deliberate and commented. Collapsing it into `compileAccess` would thread that exception through the general funnel to delete three lines: rearranging complexity, not removing it.

**The benchmark's placement itself stands.** It is the owner's decision, and branch protection on `main` already requires `[Release policy, Fast CI, Benchmark]`. Only the documentation was wrong.

reviews.body:
The advisory perf gate has failed on two PRs containing **no DSP code whatsoever** — #519 (docs only, +59.7%) and #524 (build tooling only, +66.5%). A gate that fires on documentation changes stops being read, so it's worth establishing what it's actually measuring.

## It isn't jitter, and it isn't the runner

Both measurement phases were internally *tight* — ~1.2% stddev each — and simply disagreed with each other. And in the same CI run, two large FIR benchmarks agreed across those same two phases to within 0.15%:

| benchmark | base min | head min | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `bench_fir::test_bench_execute[409600]` | 19,135,333 ns | 19,107,997 ns | **−0.14%** |
| `bench_fir::test_bench_execute[819200]` | 38,290,100 ns | 38,288,683 ns | **−0.004%** |
| `bench_Resampler::test_bench_execute_decim_64k` | 1,104,593 ns | 1,839,419 ns | **+66.5%** |

So the runner was neither throttled nor systematically biased against the head — which were my first two hypotheses, and both are wrong. The C benchmark shifted identically (58.44 → 35.12 MSa/s), so it isn't a Python-layer artifact either.

What's left is a benchmark that lands in one of **two internally-stable states ~1.66× apart**, fixed per process. That's the signature of memory layout — allocation alignment or hugepage backing — not of code.

## Why exempt rather than fix

It doesn't reproduce here: **448 µs ± 0.2% across 8 separate processes** on the reference machine. Without a local repro, any change to the benchmark would be a guess dressed as a fix, and would also break comparability with the published v0.10.1→v0.37.3 history.

Note that jm already compares the **`min`** sample rather than the mean, precisely because means are noisy on shared runners (`_bench.py::_bench_metric`) — and it still fires, because bimodality moves the floor itself. No choice of statistic rescues this one.

## The change

One line, via jm's own mechanism (`bench --check --allow`): still measured, still reported with its delta, just unable to fail the build. The list sits in the Makefile next to `BENCH_THRESHOLD` — the Makefile is the single driver for the gate (#524) — and the comment requires each entry to justify why the *measurement*, not the code, is untrustworthy. Exemptions are blind spots; this one is worth it, a permanently-ignored gate is not.

Verified against jm's comparator with the real CI numbers:

```
allow=no  -> status=regressed  delta=66.5%
allow=yes -> status=allowed    delta=66.5%
```

reviews.body:
Corrects a claim I merged one turn earlier in #142. One documentation file, read-only investigation.

## What was wrong

The note said a DB-side `CHECK`/trigger was **owed** to make the invariant structural, and deferred applying it because the database was under continuous concurrent write.

Probing showed **both halves were wrong.**

## 1. The invariant is already enforced

`world_benchmark_operating_point` is a **VIEW, not a base table**, and its body ends:

```sql
  FROM world_benchmark_meta m
    JOIN world_benchmark_aggregate a ON a.meta_id = m.id
    LEFT JOIN world_benchmark_timing_aggregate t
      ON t.meta_id = a.meta_id AND t.scope = a.scope AND t.archiver = a.archiver
 WHERE m.task = 'CUBR-0087-phaseC' AND a.archiver = 'cubrim';
```

`a.archiver = 'cubrim'` is hardcoded in the view body. **I1 and I2 cannot be violated** — the view cannot emit a non-cubrim row, and no constraint could be attached to it in any case, because a view has no rows of its own to constrain. The `competitor_note` documents a property the SQL already guarantees rather than a convention a reader must uphold.

The timing join is equally tight: it matches on `meta_id`, `scope` **and** `archiver`, so speed columns on any row come from that row's own meta. No cross-meta value can enter the view through the join either.

## 2. The deferral reason was overstated

Probed directly rather than inferred from PR activity: **one active backend** (this session's own query) and **zero locks** on the target relation. The database was quiet, not busy.

## What actually remains

**I3 — and no constraint can fix it.** A comparison that spans `meta_id` is a property of how a *reader* queries `world_benchmark_timing_aggregate`; the mistake happens in the query, not in stored data. The defence is the measurement already in the note: metas 37 and 38 carry a single archiver, so a competitor comparison at those operating points **does not exist to be read**.

Nothing is owed against this view.

## Why this matters enough to correct

Leaving "enforcement owed" on `main` would have sent a future session to write a redundant constraint on an object that cannot hold one — burning time and probably ending in confusion about why `ALTER VIEW ... ADD CHECK` fails.

The decision itself is unchanged and still stands: comparisons come from the timing aggregate, only within a single `meta_id`.

Read-only throughout — no database object created, altered, or dropped; `evaluation` remains 0.

CI note: `ci.yml` path filters exclude `documentation/**`, so `ci.yml` is dispatched manually on this branch head.

## What changed

- Freezes a non-vendored CodeContests/Project CodeNet-origin Python 3 selection: 20 tasks, 40 oracle programs, 60 accepted holdout controls, and 500 globally distinct wrong-program receipts.
- Accounts for all 1,710 scoped upstream rows with a 1,690-row exclusion ledger and SHA-256 selection receipt.
- Adds pinned Parquet metadata acquisition, a gitignored selected-row cache, and a HEAD guard for the unversioned Hugging Face rows API.
- Separates provider-visible public bundles from hidden rows, requires equal-budget candidate sealing, and verifies candidate receipts before hidden scoring.
- Reports per-task and aggregate defect recall/mutation score, false kills, abstention, queries to first finding, executions, wall time, and Wilson intervals.
- Adds a manual Linux replay workflow, normal-CI manifest verification, reviewer signoff template, tests, and canonical documentation.
- Integrates current `main` (external-CI read-back, oracle provenance, evidence bundles, generator ledger, atomic apply, and runc/runsc hostile proofs) and updates `docs/NEXT_STEPS.md` to distinguish shipped work from the remaining gates.

## Why

The synthetic corpus is too small to support real-course generalization or search-superiority claims. This branch creates a reproducible, license-cautious evaluation boundary without vendoring contest descriptions, tests, or program sources and without executing untrusted code on the host.

reviews.title: Build the frozen real-corpus evaluation

reviews.body:
## Summary

**My gzip diagnosis in #448 was wrong, and the diagnostic I added in the same PR is what proved it.** The run printed the bytes that actually arrived:

```
First bytes: "id","schema","name","aliases","birth_date","countries","addresses",...
```

Plain CSV, not gzip. The headers are **quoted** — `"name"`, not `name` — and the guard's regex required a bare `name` between commas, so it saw `,"name",` and refused a perfectly good file. `csv.DictReader` strips those quotes, so the parser was never the problem; only my shell check was.

## What changed

- The header check allows optional quotes: `(^|,)"?[Nn]ame"?(,|$)`.
- The comment at the guard now records what actually happened rather than the theory it was written to confirm.
- `--compressed` **stays** — correct practice for this mirror and harmless — but I want it on the record that it was not the cause of anything.

## Verification

| Body | Result |
|---|---|
| `"id","schema","name","aliases"` (what the mirror actually serves) | accept |
| `id,schema,name,aliases` (unquoted) | accept |
| `"Name","Regime"` (quoted leading name column) | accept |
| `"id","schema","caption"` (quoted, no name column) | reject |
| HTML error page | reject |
| gzip stream | reject |

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that changes existing behavior)
- [ ] Risk data / baseline change (countries, activities, materials, FATF flags)
- [ ] Documentation / governance docs
- [x] CI / automation / tooling

## Compliance impact

Should complete the restoration of Australia DFAT and Switzerland SECO to the daily screen. Until it lands, both remain absent, the run reports the outage honestly and fails red — the correct behaviour, and not a silent gap.

No matching logic, threshold, list content or benchmark floor changes.

## Note on how this went

Two wrong diagnoses on one fault — an egress hole, then gzip — both corrected by evidence rather than argument. What made the difference was making the failure **state what it saw** instead of only that it was unhappy. That is exactly the principle the rest of today's sweep applied to the engine, applied here to my own code.

The remaining unknown is unchanged and I'm not pre-judging it: AU/CH carry **provisional** floors of 500 that have never been measured, because the lists have never loaded. If the real counts come in under 500 the gate will read corruption and refuse the whole screen. The next run reports the actual numbers, and a measured baseline is the only honest basis for setting that floor.

## Testing

- [x] `npm test` — 79/79
- [x] Header guard verified across the six body shapes above
- [ ] **A green live run — not yet.** The dispatch after merge is the proof, and I will report it either way.

## Checklist

- [x] My change is a single, focused logical unit
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or customer data are included in the diff
- [x] Updated relevant docs — the guard's comment now records the real cause
- [x] Commit messages explain the *why*
